sessions.title: Daily Prayer Practice
sessions.summary: A quiet daily practice: settle into God's presence, name the grace you seek, pray with scripture or in stillness, then look back on what happened and write a few honest lines.

segments.text: Welcome. Let yourself arrive in this place, just as you are. Settle your body so that it can be still for a while. When you are ready, take a slow, deep breath in, and let it go.
segments.why: A short, plain welcome lowers the pace before any spiritual content, which matters for someone coming straight from a busy morning or a long day.

segments.question: Breathe slowly, and settle
segments.why: Forty seconds allows four or five unhurried breaths without the silence feeling empty to a beginner.

segments.text: As you keep breathing slowly, remind yourself of something simple and true. You are not alone. God is here with you, right now, in this very place. You do not have to make that happen. Only notice it, and rest there.
segments.why: This follows the handout's invitation to place oneself in God's presence, and frames it as receiving rather than achieving.

segments.question: Rest in God's presence
segments.why: A brief second silence lets the awareness of presence sink in before the next step asks for something.

segments.text: Saint Ignatius invites us to begin every time of prayer by naming the grace we seek. So bring God a simple question: what is the grace I seek today? Don't hunt for the right answer. Just listen, and notice what word rises in you. It might be rest, or peace, or courage, or light, or mercy, or something else entirely. You have about a minute and a half to let it come.
segments.why: Giving a few example words and permission not to strain helps newcomers, and saying the length aloud lets people relax into the pause.

segments.question: What is the grace I seek?
segments.why: Ninety seconds is long enough for a word to surface and for a first word to give way to a truer one, without dragging.

segments.text: Now gently turn that word into a prayer. In your own heart, say to God: God, as I begin, I seek the grace of, and then your word. Say it once, slowly, and mean it.
segments.why: This uses the handout's form for the petition and keeps it personal and brief, as Ignatius' preludes are.

segments.question: Ask God for the grace you seek
segments.why: A short pause lets the person actually say the prayer instead of only hearing about it.

segments.text: Now there are about nine minutes for prayer. You might pray with a passage of scripture, perhaps today's retreat reading, reading it slowly and staying with any word that catches your heart. Or you might simply stay in quiet with God, carrying the grace you have asked for. If your mind wanders, that is all right. Just come back gently. A soft sound will tell you when the time is over.
segments.why: Offering both ways to pray, with reassurance about distraction, lets the person enter the long silence without worrying about doing it right or watching the clock.

segments.question: Pray with scripture, or rest in quiet with God
segments.why: Nine minutes is the heart of the practice: enough to go below the surface, while keeping the whole practice under twenty minutes on most days.

segments.text: Gently let your prayer come to a close. Take a breath. Before you move on, thank God for this time, however it went.
segments.why: A soft ending with thanks marks the change from prayer to reflection without judging the prayer time.

segments.text: Saint Ignatius suggests looking back over the time you have just spent in prayer, with one simple question: what happened here? Perhaps a word or phrase caught your heart. Perhaps God stirred a memory or an image. Notice too what you felt: hopeful or sad, afraid or at peace. Some moments may have drawn you closer to God, and others may have felt heavy or far away. Both are worth writing down. The question will be on the screen, and you have about three minutes to write a few honest lines.
segments.why: It asks the journal question aloud, names consolation and desolation in plain words without jargon, and says how long the pause lasts.

segments.question: What happened in my prayer today?
prompts: A word or phrase that caught my heart was…
A memory or image that came to me…
I felt drawn toward God, or away, when…
segments.why: Three minutes is enough to write two or three honest sentences by hand or on a phone, and the prompts follow the handout's three suggestions plus the direction of the feelings.

segments.text: Thank you, God, for being with me in this time, and for whatever you gave me here, even what I don't yet understand. Stay close to me through the rest of this day. Amen.
segments.why: A brief spoken thanksgiving gives a clear, restful ending and joins the prayer to the day ahead.

segments.question: Rest a moment before you go
segments.why: A final short silence keeps the practice from ending abruptly.

sessions.title: Weekly Review of Prayer
sessions.summary: Once a week, settle before God, read back over your daily notes, and write down how God has been moving in your heart and your life, so that looking back helps you go forward.

segments.text: Welcome to this weekly review. Find a still place, and let your body settle. Take a slow, deep breath, and let it go. Remember that God is here with you now, just as God has been with you all week.
segments.why: It opens the same way as the daily practice so the weekly review feels familiar, while turning attention toward the whole week.

segments.question: Breathe, and rest in God's presence
segments.why: Forty-five seconds is enough for a person to arrive before they are asked to look back.

segments.text: Before you look back, ask God for light. You might pray: God, help me to see this week the way you see it, with honesty and with kindness.
segments.why: Asking for light before reviewing follows the Examen, and it frames the review as gentle rather than self-critical.

segments.question: Ask God for light to see
segments.why: A short pause lets the person make the request their own.

segments.text: Now your notes from this week's prayer are there for you to read. Take about three minutes to read them slowly, one day at a time. You don't need to analyze anything yet. Just notice what stands out, a word that returns, a feeling that repeats, a moment you had forgotten. A soft sound will end the pause.
segments.why: Asking for receptive reading first, and not analysis, lets patterns surface on their own, the way Ignatian repetition returns to where something was happening.

segments.question: Read your notes from this week slowly
segments.why: Three minutes gives time to read five to seven short entries without rushing.

segments.text: Now ask yourself: what has God been doing in me this week? Where did I feel drawn toward God, more alive, more hopeful, more at peace? And where did things feel heavy, restless, or far from God? Both are part of the story. The question will be on the screen, and you have about three minutes to write.
segments.why: This puts consolation and desolation in plain words and asks the journal question aloud with its length.

segments.question: What has happened in this week's movement of God within my heart and my life?
prompts: A word or theme that kept returning…
I felt closest to God when…
It felt heavy or distant when…
Something in my life that changed…
segments.why: Three minutes allows an honest paragraph, and the prompts guide the person from patterns in prayer to their effect in daily life, as the handout asks.

segments.text: Looking back helps us keep moving forward. As you think about the week ahead, what would you like to carry with you, or ask of God? Perhaps a grace you want to keep seeking, or a word to hold on to. The question will be on the screen, and you have about two minutes.
segments.why: This carries out the handout's point that reviewing serves forward growth, and it ends the review on hope, not assessment.

segments.question: What do I want to carry into the coming week?
prompts: The grace I want to keep asking for is…
A word I want to hold on to…
God, in the week ahead, I ask…
segments.why: A shorter two-minute pause fits a single forward-looking intention.

segments.text: Thank you, God, for walking with me through this week, in the bright moments and the hard ones. Thank you for all you are doing in me, seen and unseen. Lead me on into the days ahead. Amen.
segments.why: A brief thanksgiving gathers the whole week before God and gives the review a warm, clear ending.

segments.question: Rest a moment before you go
segments.why: A final short stillness lets the review settle before the person returns to their day.

sessions.title: Your Life's Faith Story
sessions.summary: A thirty-minute guided life review. After settling and asking the Holy Spirit to guide memory and emotion, you ask for the grace to remember the fragments of your life in a way that reveals the patterns leading toward wholeness with God. You then move through six areas, writing after each one: childhood and family, the people and events that made a difference, the seasons of your life, where God was present or absent, your gifts and struggles, and God's voice in your story. The session ends with an honest conversation with God and a brief thanksgiving. Adapted from a retreat handout based on Margaret Silf's Inner Compass.

segments.text: Welcome. Find a place where you can sit comfortably, with something to write on close at hand. Let your shoulders drop. Take a slow breath in, and let it go. For the next half hour, you are going to look back over your life, not to judge it, but to see it with God. Let's begin by resting for a moment in God's presence.
segments.why: The opening names the length and purpose right away, so the person can commit to thirty minutes and put down any fear of being judged.

segments.question: Breathe, and rest in God's presence
segments.why: Just under half a minute gives time for a few slow breaths before any memory work begins.

segments.text: Holy Spirit, come and guide this remembering. Direct my memory to what matters, and hold my emotions gently as they rise. Show me my life as you see it.
segments.why: The handout asks the Spirit to direct both memory and emotion, so the voice prays that request plainly in the first person, and the listener can make it their own.

segments.text: What you write today is just for you. You can write sentences, make a list, sketch a timeline of the decades, or draw images and symbols. If you ever share any of it, you share only what you choose.
segments.why: Saying early that the writing is private and can take any form removes pressure before the first pause.

segments.text: Remembering means gathering up again what has been scattered or broken. So ask God now for the grace of this time: to remember the fragments of your life in a way that shows the patterns, the threads that have been drawing you toward wholeness with God. Ask for it in your own words, quietly.
segments.why: The handout's idea of remembering as re-membering is put in plain words, and the grace is named as a specific request, as Saint Ignatius asks in the petition.

segments.question: Ask for the grace to see the patterns of your life
segments.why: A little under a minute is enough to put the request into one's own words without the session losing momentum.

segments.text: Let's begin at the beginning. Think of the family you were born into, and the people who were close to you as a child. Who comes to mind first? How did they shape the person you have become, for good, and perhaps in harder ways too? The question will be on the screen. Take about three minutes, and a soft sound will end the pause.
segments.why: The first area starts with one person who comes to mind, which is an easy way in, and explains once how the pauses work.

segments.question: Who from your family and childhood shaped who you are, and how?
prompts: The first face that comes to mind is…
A childhood memory that still matters…
Something I carry from home, for better or worse…
segments.why: Three minutes lets someone name two or three people with a line each; the area matters but should not use up the time needed for the heavier sections.

segments.text: Now widen the circle. Think of the events and people that made a real difference in your life. Some may go back before you were born, a grandparent's choice, a family move. Some are recent, and some are still with you. What difference did they make? The question is on the screen. Take about three minutes.
segments.why: Concrete examples of influences from before one's birth help the listener grasp an idea that is easy to pass over.

segments.question: Which events and people made an important difference in your life, and how?
prompts: Someone still with me who matters…
segments.why: Three minutes is enough to jot a short list with a word on each difference made.

segments.text: Now look at the seasons of your life. There have been joys and losses, victories and failures, times of trial, and times of healing and change. You might sketch them decade by decade, or simply name the seasons that come to you. Then ask yourself which of them seems most significant. This one gets more time, about five minutes.
segments.why: The voice suggests the timeline here because this area covers the most ground, and says up front that the pause is longer.

segments.question: What have been the seasons of your life, and which seems most significant?
prompts: Decade by decade: a joy and a sorrow from each…
A time of healing or transformation…
segments.why: This area has the most to remember, so it gets nearly five minutes, enough to sketch a whole timeline.

segments.text: Stay with those seasons, and look at them now with God in mind. Where do you notice God was present? Where did God seem absent? Some times may have strengthened you or prepared you to grow. There may also be griefs and wounds that still weigh on you. Go gently here. Write only what you are comfortable writing; a single word is enough, and you can leave something unwritten and simply hold it before God. You have about five minutes.
segments.why: This is the heaviest area, so it builds directly on the timeline just made and gives clear permission to write little or nothing before the pause begins.

segments.question: Looking back, where was God present, or absent, in the seasons of your life?
prompts: I sense God was near when…
A hard time that prepared me to grow…
A grief or wound I still carry (only if you wish)…
segments.why: Discerning presence and absence while touching old wounds needs unhurried time, so this pause matches the longest one.

segments.text: Whatever came up, you don't have to carry it alone right now. Lay down your pen for a moment. If something hurt, let God hold it with you. Breathe slowly.
segments.why: A gentle word after the hard area lets feelings settle before the person turns to something new.

segments.question: Breathe, and let God hold what came up
segments.why: A short breathing space marks the move from wounds to gifts, so the next area does not feel abrupt.

segments.text: Now turn to yourself as you are. What are your gifts, your temperament, the traits others see in you? How does God seem to work through what you are good at? And where do your struggles get in the way, like stones in a stream? The question is on the screen. Take about three minutes.
segments.why: The image of stones in a stream makes the handout's phrase about God's flow easy to hold on a single hearing.

segments.question: Who are you, how does God work through your gifts, and where do your struggles get in the way?
prompts: A gift God seems to use…
A struggle that blocks the flow…
Who I understand myself to be…
segments.why: Three minutes is enough to name a gift and a struggle honestly without turning it into a self-assessment.

segments.text: Last, listen for God's voice across your story. Where have you heard God quietly, in a still, small voice? Where have you felt God's presence strongly, guiding you? And where do you long for more of God's grace and love? Take about three minutes.
segments.why: The final area ends on longing, which leads naturally into the conversation with God that follows.

segments.question: Where have you heard God's still, small voice, felt God's guidance, and longed for more?
prompts: A quiet moment when God spoke…
A time God's guidance was strong…
Where I long for more of God's love…
segments.why: Three minutes lets the person gather a few moments of God's voice from all they have already written.

segments.text: Now set your writing aside. Look over what you have written, or simply remember it. Then speak honestly with God about whatever has risen to the surface, as one friend speaks to another. Ask, Lord, what do you want me to notice? Then listen. You have two minutes of quiet.
segments.why: The handout's closing question is framed as an Ignatian colloquy, a conversation between friends, and the person hears how long the quiet will last.

segments.question: Lord, what do you want me to notice?
segments.why: Two minutes leaves room both to speak honestly and to listen, without adding more writing.

segments.text: Thank you, God, for every part of this story, the bright threads and the broken ones. Gather what I have remembered today into your hands, and keep drawing me toward wholeness in you. Amen. You might return to these pages another day, when something new comes to mind.
segments.why: The close gives thanks, returns to the grace of wholeness, and leaves the review open, since a life story is rarely finished in one sitting.

sessions.title: The Examen
sessions.summary: A gentle fifteen-minute end-of-day prayer in the way of Saint Ignatius, looking back over the day with God to see where love was given, where it was received, and what grace to ask for tomorrow.

segments.text: Good evening. The day is nearly over, and you have come to rest in it for a little while. You can lie down or sit, whichever is kindest to you tonight. Let your eyes close if you like. There is nothing to achieve here. This is a short prayer from Saint Ignatius, called the Examen, and it is simply a way of looking back over the day with God, not to deliver a verdict, but to notice.
segments.why: A soft welcome that lowers the stakes for a tired listener and frames the Examen as noticing rather than judging.

segments.text: Let us begin with a few slow breaths. Feel the weight of your body, wherever it is resting. Notice whatever you are carrying, tiredness, worry, relief, and you don't need to fix any of it. Just breathe.
segments.why: Brief bodily cue before the first silence so the pause has something gentle to do.

segments.question: Breathe slowly, and let the day settle
segments.why: Thirty seconds allows four or five slow breaths without drifting toward sleep.

segments.text: You are not alone in this looking back. God has been with you through every hour of today, and already knows all of it. So we ask for help to see. Pray with me quietly. God, you have been with me throughout this day. Help me become aware of you now, and let me see this day as you see it.
segments.why: The Examen begins with grace, not introspection, so the petition comes before any reviewing.

segments.question: Rest in God's presence
segments.why: A short rest lets the prayer land before moving on.

segments.text: Before anything else, we look for what was given. It might be something large, or something very ordinary. A good conversation. A cup of tea. Someone who made you laugh. A moment outside, a piece of music, your body carrying you through. If today was hard, you don't have to pretend otherwise. Simply ask, what was given to me today? And let whatever comes, come.
segments.why: Gratitude comes early because life is received as gift; the concrete examples help a tired mind find something quickly.

segments.question: What was given to me today?
segments.why: Fifty seconds gives time for two or three gifts to surface and be savoured.

segments.text: Now we walk back through the day together, gently, as if watching a recording. You don't need to examine every minute. Look for the moments that carry some feeling: irritation, a sudden peace, anxiety, hope, loneliness, tenderness. Your feelings and desires are telling you something. Saint Ignatius spoke of consolation and desolation. Consolation isn't just feeling good. It is whatever moves you toward faith, hope and love, toward courage and connection, even something hard, like an awkward apology. Desolation isn't just feeling bad. It is whatever pulls you inward, toward fear, resentment, numbness, even something pleasant that left you empty. For now, just notice, before you judge.
segments.why: The heart of the Examen, so consolation and desolation are explained here, briefly and in plain words, before the replay begins.

segments.text: Go back to this morning. Waking up. The first thoughts of the day. Breakfast, getting ready, getting out of the door. What was happening in you?
segments.why: Short, concrete cues guide the replay through an ordinary day without crowding it.

segments.question: This morning: what was stirring in me?
segments.why: Forty seconds per part of the day keeps the replay moving while allowing a moment to be revisited.

segments.text: Now the middle of the day. Work, or study, or the tasks of home. The people you spoke to. Lunch. Was there a moment that lifted you, or one that weighed on you?
segments.why: Naming common midday moments helps the listener locate real memories quickly.

segments.question: The middle of the day: what lifted me, what weighed on me?
segments.why: Matches the rhythm of the morning pause so the replay feels steady.

segments.text: And the afternoon and the evening, right up to now, lying here. Where did you feel most alive? Where did you close yourself off?
segments.why: Bringing the replay up to the present moment grounds it and introduces the key contrasting questions.

segments.question: The afternoon and evening, until now
segments.why: Completes the replay with equal time for the last part of the day.

segments.text: Now choose one moment that stands out, whichever one seems to ask for attention, and stay with it. What were you wanting then? Where did it lead you, toward peace or toward restlessness? Did God feel near, or far away? Just let it be seen.
segments.why: Ignatius returns to where there was movement, so the listener dwells on one moment rather than skimming many.

segments.question: Stay with one moment, and let it be seen
segments.why: The longest review silence, since staying with one moment is where the real noticing happens.

segments.text: If you'd like to, you can write a line or two now, about the moment you are most grateful for today, and the moment you are least grateful for. The question will be on the screen, and you have about a minute and a quarter. Writing is entirely optional. It is just as good to keep your eyes closed and hold those two moments before God. A soft sound will end the pause.
segments.why: An optional short journal pause gathers the review into the simple two-moment variation, with clear permission not to write.

segments.question: For what moment today am I most grateful, and least grateful?
prompts: The moment I'm most grateful for was...
The moment I'd rather forget was...
What I noticed in me then...
segments.why: Seventy-five seconds is enough for two short sentences on a phone, and not so long that eyes-closed listeners feel stranded.

segments.text: Now, gently, is there something from today you regret? Perhaps impatience, a sharp word, someone you ignored, a resentment you fed. Bring that one thing before God, honestly, but without beating yourself up. You might say, I see what I did. I see how it hurt. I am sorry. Forgive me.
segments.why: One particular thing, named plainly, keeps this honest without turning it into self-loathing.

segments.question: Bring it before God, and ask forgiveness
segments.why: Forty seconds for a sincere, private word of sorrow.

segments.text: And ask, underneath it, what was I actually seeking? Sometimes there is fear under anger, or a longing to feel valued under envy, or fear of failing under putting things off. This does not excuse anything. But it can show you something that guilt alone never would. Ask God to help you understand.
segments.why: The question of the deeper desire links the Examen to discernment and moves beyond mere guilt.

segments.question: What was I really seeking?
segments.why: A shorter pause, because insight here often comes as a glimpse rather than an answer.

segments.text: And if there was something good today, a patience you didn't expect of yourself, a kindness that came easily, receive it too. Not as a trophy, but as grace. Simply say thank you.
segments.why: Receiving the good as gift balances the review and guards against both pride and scrupulosity.

segments.question: Receive the good as grace
segments.why: A brief breath of thanksgiving before turning toward tomorrow.

segments.text: Now look ahead to tomorrow. What is actually coming? A meeting, a difficult conversation, family, a decision, a worry you already know will visit. Given what you have seen tonight, what grace will you need? Make it concrete. Not, make me better, but something like, when I talk to that person, help me listen instead of trying to win. Or simply, give me patience.
segments.why: Concrete examples help the listener name a specific, usable grace rather than a vague resolution.

segments.question: What is coming tomorrow?
segments.why: A short pause to picture tomorrow before naming the grace.

segments.text: If you'd like to, write down the grace you are asking for tomorrow, so it is there for you in the morning. The question will be on the screen, and you have about a minute and a half. Again, writing is optional. You can simply stay with your eyes closed and ask for it. A soft sound will end the pause.
segments.why: The one main journal pause is kept for tomorrow's grace, because having it written down helps in the morning.

segments.question: What grace do I need for tomorrow?
prompts: Lord, when that happens, help me...
The grace I ask for is...
segments.why: Ninety seconds is enough to write one honest sentence, even when tired.

segments.text: Now we place tomorrow, and everything in today, into God's hands. Let us pray slowly together the prayer Jesus gave us.
segments.why: A short entrusting line leads naturally into the traditional ending of the Examen.

segments.text: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.
segments.why: The traditional English text, broken into short sentences so it can be spoken slowly and prayed along with.

segments.text: Thank you for this day, and for this time. May God, who has been with you in every hour of it, keep watch over you through the night. Rest now, held and forgiven, and sleep in peace.
segments.why: A brief blessing for sleep that ends in stillness, with nothing further to do.

sessions.title: Prayer Over My Dossier
sessions.summary: A prayer of praise over the plain facts of your life, writing down your family, places and traits one group at a time and turning each into thanks to the God who chose them for you. Adapted from a retreat worksheet (Prayer Unit 2, Day 3: Prayer Over My Dossier).

segments.text: Welcome. Today you will pray over the plain facts of your life: names, dates, places, the shape of your family and of yourself. Saint Ignatius believed God can be found in all things, and that includes the ordinary details of who you are. For now, simply let yourself arrive.
segments.why: Names the unusual shape of this prayer at the start so the listener is not surprised when a prayer turns into writing facts.

segments.question: Breathe, and let your body settle
segments.why: Thirty seconds allows four or five slow breaths before God is addressed.

segments.text: Now become aware that God is here. Not a distant God, but your Maker, the One who thought of you before anyone knew your name. Rest for a moment before the One who made you, and who is making you still.
segments.why: Places the person before God as Maker, the image the whole session returns to at the end.

segments.text: Ask now for the grace of this prayer. You might say it simply: Lord, let me see the facts of my life as your gifts, and let me thank and praise you for choosing me, here, in this time, with these people. Or ask it in your own words.
segments.why: Gives the petition in plain words the listener can borrow or replace with their own.

segments.question: Ask for the grace in your own words
segments.why: A short pause is enough to ask for one grace, since the long work of the session lies ahead.

segments.text: A word before we begin. What you write is just for you. Write as much or as little as you like. If something is unknown to you, or too painful to write today, it's fine to leave that line blank. God already knows it, and holds it gently. At each step the question will be on the screen, and a soft sound will end the pause.
segments.why: Gives explicit permission to leave lines blank before the family questions begin, since adoption, estrangement or loss can make them painful.

segments.text: Let's begin with your father. Whatever you know of him, and whatever your story with him, he is part of how God brought you into being. Write his full name, his birth date, and where he was born. As you write, you might simply say, thank you. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Acknowledges that the story with a father may be complicated before asking only for simple facts.

segments.question: What do you know of your father?
segments.why: Two minutes is enough to write three facts and lift a brief word of thanks.

segments.text: Now your mother. Let her name come to you slowly. Write her full name, her birth date, and her birthplace, and as you write, lift your mind to God, who gave you life through her. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Mirrors the father's segment so the rhythm of writing and then praising becomes familiar.

segments.question: What do you know of your mother?
segments.why: The same length as the father's pause keeps the simple facts brisk.

segments.text: Now write about yourself, as if for the first time. Your full name, the day and place you were born. Your gender, your race and ethnicity. The color of your hair and eyes, the build of your body. None of this was an accident to God. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Reads the fields as a gentle walk through the self rather than a form, and ends on God's intention.

segments.question: Who am I, in plain facts?
prompts: My hair color, eye color and build
segments.why: These facts come quickly, so two minutes leaves room for a moment of wonder.

segments.text: Now your brothers and sisters, if you have them. Write each name and birth date. If you have none, or if some are lost to you, you might write that too, or simply rest. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Anticipates only children and lost siblings so no one feels the question does not fit them.

segments.question: Who are my brothers and sisters?
prompts: First sibling: name and birth date
Second sibling: name and birth date
segments.why: Two minutes covers most families, and anyone without siblings can simply rest.

segments.text: Now take a little longer with your family's story. What details matter? A move, a loss, a marriage, a faith handed down, a hardship survived. Write what seems significant, and let each thing become thanks where you can. You have two and a half minutes.
segments.why: Offers concrete examples so an open-ended question has a place to start, and says thanks is asked only where it can be given.

segments.question: What are the significant details of my family's story?
prompts: A move or a turning point
A faith or tradition handed down
segments.why: Family details need more recollection than names, so this pause runs longer.

segments.text: Now the places you have lived. Let them come back one by one: the towns and streets, the houses and rooms. God was with you in each of them. Write them down, in whatever order they come. You have two and a half minutes.
segments.why: Evokes sensory memory of places so the listener recalls them rather than simply listing them.

segments.question: Where have I lived?
prompts: Where I was born and grew up
segments.why: The places of a lifetime take longer to remember, so this pause matches the family details.

segments.text: Last among the facts, your extended family. Grandparents, aunts and uncles, cousins, the people who were like family to you. Write whom you remember, and thank God for them. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Includes chosen family so the question fits many kinds of lives.

segments.question: Who is my extended family?
segments.why: Two minutes closes the section on facts at a steady pace.

segments.text: Now set your pen down and look over everything you have written. These are the choices God made for you and in you. Simply look, and ponder, and let praise rise if it will. Take a quiet moment.
segments.why: Turns the listener from writing to pondering before the more personal traits begin.

segments.question: Look over it all, and ponder God's choices for you
segments.why: Forty-five seconds is enough to read back over the page without losing momentum.

segments.text: Now we turn from facts to traits. Some things were formed in you before you had any choice: the place you grew up, your temperament, self-assured or anxious, your mind, the languages you speak, your habits of study, the things you love to do. Write six of them. You have nearly four minutes.
segments.why: Speaks the worksheet's examples aloud so the listener has them in hand, since nothing can be looked back at.

segments.question: What was formed in me before I had a choice?
prompts: The world I grew up in
segments.why: Six reflective items need close to four minutes to name them and offer thanks.

segments.text: Now think of what came to you through your parents or your wider family. A laugh, a temper, a gift for music, a way of worrying. Some you are glad of, some you would rather not have. Write six, honestly. You have nearly four minutes.
segments.why: Mixes welcome and unwelcome examples so honesty feels allowed from the start.

segments.question: What have I inherited from my family?
segments.why: The same length as the other trait pauses keeps the four sets in balance.

segments.text: Now name six qualities you particularly like in yourself. Perhaps you are quiet, or outgoing, thorough, sensitive to others, energetic, able to get a great deal done. Receive each as a gift from the One who makes you, and thank God for it. You have nearly four minutes.
segments.why: Frames self-appreciation as receiving a gift, which eases the discomfort many people feel in naming their good qualities.

segments.question: What do I like in myself, as God's gift?
prompts: Another gift I see in myself
segments.why: Gives time to write each quality and turn it into praise.

segments.text: Now, gently, the qualities you don't particularly like. Your height, perhaps, or an attitude you can't shake, an illness you live with, a voice inside that speaks poorly of you. Name six honestly, without contempt for yourself. You don't have to praise what still hurts. If it helps, pray each one this way: for this too, I place it in your hands. You have nearly four minutes.
segments.why: The slowest and gentlest introduction of the session, and it offers a way to pray these traits that is truthful without forcing praise.

segments.question: What don't I like in myself, that I can place in God's hands?
prompts: An illness or limit I live with
For this too, I place it in your hands
segments.why: The final prompt models the prayer itself, so the pause ends in offering rather than self-criticism.

segments.text: Now rest from writing. Consider this: God loved you before you existed. And God did not finish making you long ago. God is creating you still, in this very hour, and the Spirit still hopes for you, that you will grow until you love as God loves. Stay with that, and marvel.
segments.why: Comes directly after the hardest traits so that the unfinished parts of the person are seen as God's ongoing work.

segments.question: Marvel that God is still making you
segments.why: A full minute of quiet lets this central truth settle after so much writing.

segments.text: If you like, take a little time for anything else that has come to you: a memory, an image, a few words, even a small sketch. Or simply sit. This last pause is yours, a little over a minute.
segments.why: Presents the worksheet's last page as optional so a tired person can simply rest.

segments.question: Is there anything more I want to remember, write or draw?
segments.why: Kept short because it is optional and the session is nearly complete.

segments.text: Now gather all of it and offer it back. Thank God for your father and mother, your family, the places that held you, and the person you are and are becoming. For all of this, praise and thanks to you, my God.
segments.why: Gathers every group into one thanksgiving and echoes the worksheet's refrain of praise.

segments.text: May the God who made you keep making you. May Christ walk with you in every ordinary detail of your life. And may the Holy Spirit bring you to love as God loves. Amen.
segments.why: A brief blessing that returns to the image of God still creating and sends the person into the day.

sessions.title: Meditation on My Birth
sessions.summary: A prayer of memory and imagination, in the manner of Ignatian imaginative contemplation, in which you stand beside God your Creator as an observer at your own birth and hear how deeply you are loved. Adapted from a meditation by Dr. Eileen C. Burke-Sullivan, Creighton University.

segments.text: Welcome. This prayer is a meditation on your own birth, made with memory and with imagination, in the way Saint Ignatius taught people to enter a scene as if they were really there. Find a place where you can be still. Let your feet rest flat on the floor, and let your hands be open or at rest in your lap. Now begin to breathe slowly, in and out, letting each breath be a little longer than the one before.
segments.why: Grounds the body first and names the kind of prayer so the listener knows what is coming.

segments.question: Breathe slowly until you are somewhat at peace
segments.why: Forty-five seconds allows six or seven slow breaths, enough to settle without feeling idle.

segments.text: You don't need to be perfectly calm. Somewhat at peace is enough. God is already here, closer to you than your own breath. Now ask for what you desire in this prayer. You might say, in your own words: Lord, give me the gift of memory, or of imagination, so that I may be present at my own birth. And let me come to know how much you love me.
segments.why: Names the petition plainly, as Ignatius asks, and lowers the bar for how settled one must feel.

segments.question: Ask God for this grace in your own words
segments.why: A short pause lets the person make the petition their own rather than just hearing it.

segments.text: Now let your mind turn to what you have been told. Families keep stories about a birth. Where was your mother when her labor began? At home, at work, on the way somewhere? Did you come early, or late, or just on time? Was it a long labor, or did you arrive suddenly? Let whatever you have heard come back to you, without hurrying.
segments.why: Concrete questions give memory something to catch on before imagination begins.

segments.text: If no one ever told you these things, that's all right. You can imagine, drawing on what you know of how babies are born, even from a film or a television show. If you were adopted, or never knew your birth parents, you may imagine them as you would like them to have been. And if the story of your birth is a painful one, you don't have to go into the details. You can simply stay with God's presence, or stop at any point. This prayer is meant to be gentle.
segments.why: Said plainly and before the silence so that no one is left out or pressed into a painful memory.

segments.question: Recall or imagine the story of your birth
segments.why: A full minute lets family stories surface or a picture form without rushing.

segments.text: Now, in your imagination, go to the place where you were born. You are there as you are today, an observer, standing quietly. And God your Creator is standing at your side. You may not see God. But you know God is near, the way you know the warmth of someone standing close beside you. Let yourself feel that warmth.
segments.why: Establishes God's presence by warmth before any detail of the scene, so the whole contemplation happens in company.

segments.question: Stand with God at your side
segments.why: Short silences between each movement keep the pace slow without losing the thread.

segments.text: Look around the room. Notice what it is like, the light, the walls, the bed where your mother lies. There are people caring for her, a doctor and nurses, or a midwife and her helpers. They are busy and focused, all their attention on your mother. They cannot see you as you are now, and they cannot see God. Only you and God are watching.
segments.why: The composition of place, with the observers unseen, makes the scene private between the person and God.

segments.question: Look around the room
segments.why: Time to let the room take shape in the imagination.

segments.text: Now listen. Hear your mother in labor, breathing hard, perhaps crying out, perhaps suddenly catching her breath. Your father may be there, or he may not. But someone is beside her, encouraging her, telling her she can do this, that it won't be long now.
segments.why: Moves from sight to hearing, as Ignatian contemplation does, and leaves the father's presence open.

segments.question: Listen to the sounds of the room
segments.why: Hearing takes a little time to imagine; thirty seconds keeps momentum.

segments.text: And now you see the child you were, being born. So tiny. So defenseless. Coming into a strange, bright, cold new world. Someone lifts you, and helps you take your very first breath. Watch that little one breathe.
segments.why: Very short sentences slow the voice at the moment of birth itself.

segments.question: Watch the child you were take a first breath
segments.why: Lets the tenderness of the image register before moving on.

segments.text: A nurse takes you now. She washes you, weighs you, measures you, and wraps you, getting ready to lay you in your mother's arms.
segments.why: A brief ordinary moment that sets up the pause in which God steps forward.

segments.question: Watch the child being washed and wrapped
segments.why: A shorter silence, since this is a transition rather than the heart of the scene.

segments.text: But just for a moment, before you are handed to your mother, God steps forward. God takes you, that newborn, into the divine arms. And God gazes at you with complete love. See God's delight. God is almost playful, full of joy at simply holding you. Stay and watch this for a while.
segments.why: The turning point of the prayer, stated simply so the image, not the words, does the work.

segments.question: Watch God holding you with delight
segments.why: Longer silence here because this is where consolation is most likely to stir.

segments.text: Now God gives the child back, to be placed in your mother's arms. And then God turns, and looks deep into your eyes, the eyes you have now. And God says to you: You are my beloved child. I longed for the moment you would come into life. And I long even more for you to know how deeply you are loved.
segments.why: God's words are given in the first person and kept few, so they can be heard and held.

segments.question: Stay with God's gaze and God's words
segments.why: Two minutes to rest in the moment, in the spirit of Ignatian repetition and contemplatio.

segments.text: When you are ready, speak to God from your heart, as one friend speaks to another. What do you want to say to this God who loves you so completely? And do you believe what God has just told you? If you do, say so. If part of you doubts it, you can say that too. Talk with God about whatever is in your heart. You have about three minutes, and a soft sound will end the time.
segments.why: Invites honesty, including doubt, so the colloquy is real conversation rather than a correct answer.

segments.question: Speak with God from your heart
segments.why: Three minutes gives the colloquy real time, the longest pause in the prayer.

segments.text: Now let's close the prayer together. If you are able, bow toward God as we pray, slowly. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.
segments.why: The traditional words, prayed slowly with a bodily gesture, seal the prayer as an act of praise.

segments.question: Rest after the prayer
segments.why: A brief breath between prayer and review so the shift is not abrupt.

segments.text: Now take a few minutes to look back over the prayer. Writing is optional; if you'd rather simply reflect, that's fine. Before you write, you might talk for a moment with Jesus about what just happened, as you would with a friend who was there. Then, if you like, write. The first question is this: What did you feel during this prayer, and did any of it seem real to you? You have about two and a half minutes, and the question will be on the screen.
segments.why: Joins the conversation with Jesus to the first question so the review stays prayerful and within time.

segments.question: What did you feel in this prayer, and did it seem real to you?
prompts: I did, or didn't, sense a connection with my Creator because…
Talking with Jesus about it, I said…
segments.why: Two and a half minutes allows a short word with Jesus and two or three honest sentences.

segments.text: Now the second question. What did you see in your imagination, what did you think, and what do you long for from this kind of prayer? If you were disappointed, or nothing much seemed to happen, write that honestly too. It belongs to your prayer as much as anything else. You have about two and a half minutes.
segments.why: Explicitly welcomes disappointment so the person can notice desolation without shame.

segments.question: What did you see, what did you think, and what do you long for from this prayer?
prompts: What I long for in prayer like this is…
segments.why: Enough time to describe the scene and name a longing, the seed of the next prayer.

segments.text: One last question. Were there distractions? When did they come, what were they, and how did you handle them? Everyone's prayer has distractions, and simply noticing them helps. You have two minutes.
segments.why: Normalizes distraction before asking about it, keeping the tone free of judgment.

segments.question: Were there distractions? When, from what, and how did you handle them?
segments.why: A shorter pause since this question is usually quick to answer.

segments.text: Thank you for praying today. Whatever you saw or didn't see, what God said is still true: you are God's beloved child, and God longed for you to be born. Carry that with you into the rest of your day, or into your rest tonight. Amen.
segments.why: A brief thanksgiving that hands back God's words as the one thing to carry, whatever the prayer felt like.

sessions.title: Sleep with Prayer · 10 minutes
sessions.summary: A few verses about God's care, read slowly, with chant between: then the music carries you to sleep.

segments.text: Good night. This is a short prayer to carry you toward sleep. There is nothing left to do now, and nothing left to finish. Let the day be over. Let your body grow heavy, and let the music hold you. Between the words there will be long quiet. If you fall asleep before the end, that is exactly right.
From Psalm four. In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.

From the letter to the Philippians. Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report; if there is any virtue, and if there is any praise, think about these things.
From Psalm one hundred and twenty-one. He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

Receive the blessing given to God's people from the beginning. Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace. Sleep now, in peace.

sessions.title: Sleep with Prayer · 30 minutes
sessions.summary: Scripture about wonder and goodness, with long stretches of chant that grow longer as you drift off.

segments.text: Good night. Let the day be over now. Whatever was done today, and whatever was left undone, can rest until morning. Settle into the bed, and let it hold your weight. Breathe slowly, and let each breath out be a little longer than the one before. The God who made the stars keeps watch tonight, and does not sleep, so you may. You will hear a few words of scripture, beautiful and good to think on, with long stretches of music between. There is nothing to answer and nothing to remember. If you fall asleep before the end, that is exactly right.
From Psalm four. In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
From Psalm nineteen. The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.

From Psalm eight. When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?

From the Gospel of Matthew. Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.

From the letter to the Philippians. Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report; if there is any virtue, and if there is any praise, think about these things.
From the book of Lamentations. It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
From Psalm one hundred and thirty-one. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
From Psalm sixty-three. when I remember you on my bed, and think about you in the night watches. For you have been my help. I will rejoice in the shadow of your wings.

Receive the blessing given to God's people from the beginning. Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace. Sleep now, in peace.

sessions.title: Sleep with Prayer · 45 minutes
sessions.summary: A long, slow night prayer: the goodness of creation and of God, read gently, with chant and quiet between.

segments.text: Good night. Let the day be over now. Whatever was done today, and whatever was left undone, can rest until morning. Settle into the bed, and let it hold your weight. Breathe slowly, and let each breath out be a little longer than the one before. The God who made the stars keeps watch tonight, and does not sleep, so you may. You will hear a few words of scripture, beautiful and good to think on, with long stretches of music between. There is nothing to answer and nothing to remember. If you fall asleep before the end, that is exactly right.
From Psalm four. In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
From the book of Genesis. God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
From Psalm nineteen. The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.

From Psalm eight. When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?

From the prophet Isaiah. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. by the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, Not one is lacking.
From Psalm one hundred and four. Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches.

From the Gospel of Matthew. Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.

From the Song of Songs. For, behold, the winter is past. The rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth. The time of the singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
From Psalm twenty-seven. One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
From the prophet Zephaniah. Yahweh, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.
From Psalm one hundred and thirty-nine. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

From Psalm twenty-three. Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
From Psalm forty-six. Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth.
